metadata.title: Managing Artificial Intelligence in Archeology. An overview

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article does not analyze any ILSA micro-data (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS) and therefore does not define a sampling frame, student-level analytic sample, or any complex survey design. No plausible values (PV) or IRT/WLE scaling for achievement outcomes are computed, and no survey weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT or BRR/jackknife replicate weights) are referenced. As a result, there is no basis for specifying how weights should be applied or how replicate variance estimation would be conducted. The paper is a conceptual overview of AI in archaeology, so weighting guidance for ILSA is not applicable to its analyses.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the paper does not use any ILSA assessment data or model cognitive achievement outcomes that would require PV-based scoring. The paper is a conceptual overview of AI in archaeology and does not report an empirical student-level dataset, model training, or an explicit missing-data procedure. Therefore, missing-data handling is not reported because there is no analytic dataset construction or estimation pipeline to which such a procedure would apply.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No ILSA (or other large-scale assessment) student micro-data are used. The article provides a non-empirical overview of AI concepts, applications, and challenges in archaeology, with no analytic subsample definition, grade/domain restriction, or country-level sampling described.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This article is a conceptual overview of how artificial intelligence (including machine learning and deep learning) is used in archaeology, focusing on post-digitality, transparency, ethics, and technical challenges. It does not use any ILSA or national large-scale assessment micro-data (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS/NAEP) and does not define an assessment cycle, grade, or achievement domain. Consequently, there are no predictive targets, no trained ML models evaluated on an ILSA dataset, and no performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, AUC, RMSE) reported from an empirical modeling exercise. The paper discusses example accuracies from archaeological AI applications in general terms, but these are not tied to an ILSA dataset and are not part of a reproducible large-scale assessment analysis. Limitations therefore concern the absence of measurement, sampling, weighting, and missing-data procedures typical of ILSA-based empirical studies. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the manuscript is not an empirical ILSA-based ML study: it does not analyze student responses, plausible values, or any assessment dataset. It also does not report a sampling design, analytic sample size, country coverage, or model evaluation results. As a result, fields required for empirical large-scale assessment ML (e.g., main_findings, confounders, PV handling, missing-data handling, and ML techniques) are intentionally left empty or set to non-applicable/not-reported according to the schema rules.
